prompt: Which kind of load is the reason sharding exists, because copies of the database cannot absorb it?
hint: Think about what every copy has to receive.

choices.text: Writes
choices.why: Right: every copy must apply every write, so only splitting the data spreads them.

choices.text: Reads of recent rows
choices.why: Reads spread over replicas and caches; that is what lessons 20 and 21 are for.

choices.text: Reports that read old data once a year
choices.why: Those are reads, and archiving or a warehouse handles them.

choices.text: Too many open connections from the application
choices.why: That is a pooling problem, lesson 16, and one server still copes once it is pooled.

prompt: A team's primary is at 90% processor, and the top three statements in `pg_stat_statements` are a `SELECT` with a sequential scan, a report and a search. They propose sharding. What does the lesson say comes first?
hint: Look at what kind of statements are on top.

choices.text: Shard by the column the search filters on, since it is the most frequent
choices.why: Sharding answers write volume; these are reads, and the plans are the first suspect.

choices.text: Fix the three queries, then add replicas or a cache for the reads
choices.why: Right: the load is reads running bad plans, the cheapest items on the list.

choices.text: Buy the largest machine available and stop measuring
choices.why: A bigger machine is on the list, but after the queries, and measuring never stops.

choices.text: Partition the report's table by hash
choices.why: Hash partitioning does not help a report that reads everything; the plans come first.

prompt: In `market`, 2023 holds 221610 of the 2000000 orders and is read a few times a year. What does moving those rows out of the hot table buy?
hint: The lesson calls this archiving.

choices.text: Faster writes, because each order is now written to two places
choices.why: Archiving moves old rows once; new orders are still written to one table.

choices.text: Nothing measurable, since unread rows cost nothing
choices.why: They still cost index memory, vacuum time and restore time.

choices.text: A hot table about a ninth smaller, and the gain grows every year
choices.why: Right: 221610 is about 11% of the orders, and each year adds another old year.

choices.text: A second server to send the reports to
choices.why: That is a replica; archiving is about where old rows live.

prompt: A company must keep Brazilian customers' data in Brazil and German customers' data in Germany, and its database is small and fast. Is sharding justified?
hint: The lesson names a second reason that is not speed.

choices.text: No, because sharding is only ever a fix for too much write volume
choices.why: The lesson names data residence as a second reason, with the same mechanics.

choices.text: Yes, with the country as a shard key the law chose
choices.why: Right: the reason to pay the bill is legal rather than performance.

choices.text: No, a read replica in each country is enough
choices.why: A replica holds every row, so German data would sit in Brazil too.

choices.text: Yes, because a small database is always faster when split
choices.why: Splitting adds network trips; a small database gains no speed from it.

prompt: Order these steps from what to try first to what to try last, as the lesson ranks them by cost.
hint: Rewriting what the application knows is the most expensive.
items: Fix the queries that dominate the tally
Partition the large table on the same server
trap: Sharding before the queries are fixed spreads three bad plans over several servers.

prompt: Split by `seller_id % 4`, what percentage of all orders lands on the shard that holds seller 1?
hint: Seller 1's quarter plus a quarter of everybody else.

prompt: Why can adding more shards not cure the hot shard when the key is `seller_id`?
hint: How many shards can one seller's rows live on?

choices.text: Every row of seller 1 goes to the same shard, however many there are
choices.why: Right: one value cannot be split by a function of that value, so a quarter stays together.

choices.text: PostgreSQL limits a hash-partitioned table to four partitions, so a fifth is refused
choices.why: There is no such limit; the modulus can be any number.

choices.text: More shards means more network trips for every query
choices.why: True for fan-out queries, but not why seller 1's shard stays hot.

choices.text: Seller 1's orders are written in time order
choices.why: The order rows are written in has nothing to do with which shard they go to.

prompt: Lesson 2's workload is 50% customer order lists and 4% seller dashboards. Why does that settle the key as `customer_id`, beyond the even split?
hint: Which queries stay on one shard under each key?

choices.text: Because the seller dashboards stop working entirely once the table is split by customer
choices.why: They still work; they fan out to every shard and cost more.

choices.text: Because writes are routed by seller
choices.why: A write of one order goes to one shard under either key.

choices.text: Half the traffic then names the key and stays on one shard; only the 4% fans out
choices.why: Right: the key should be the column most of the traffic already filters by.

choices.text: Because customer ids are smaller numbers than seller ids, so they hash more evenly
choices.why: The size of the numbers is irrelevant; customer ids are in fact larger.

prompt: Sharding `order_lines` by the same key as `orders`, so that a join between them runs inside one server, is called ___.
hint: A word for living in the same place.

prompt: Match each way to route a key to a server with what it costs.
hint: Each has one weakness the lesson names.

pairs.right: even, and blind to what the values mean
a band grows hot when new keys are all high
one more lookup on every request

right_distractors: a row can only ever move with the whole table

prompt: A video platform considers sharding comments by `video_id`. One video in a thousand goes viral and gets most of the day's comments. What does the lesson predict?
hint: Compare with seller 1.

choices.text: Range routing would avoid it
choices.why: No routing function splits one value; the problem is the key.

choices.text: A hot shard: the viral video's comments all land on one server
choices.why: Right: it is the seller 1 shape, a single value large enough to fill a server.

choices.text: An even spread, because there are many videos
choices.why: Many values do not help when one of them carries most of the writes.

choices.text: Nothing, until there are a hundred shards
choices.why: With a hundred shards the viral video still sits on one of them.

prompt: In `EXPLAIN (VERBOSE)` on the coordinator, what does the `Remote SQL` line show?
hint: It is about what crosses the connection.

choices.text: The statement the shard will run, as the coordinator sends it
choices.why: Right: it is how you see whether a WHERE or a GROUP BY travels to the shard.

choices.text: The plan the shard chose
choices.why: The shard plans it on its own side; the coordinator only shows what it sends.

choices.text: The SQL the application typed, unchanged
choices.why: It is rewritten per shard, often with fewer columns or no aggregate.

choices.text: A log of the rows that came back over the connection while the query ran
choices.why: EXPLAIN without ANALYZE runs nothing, so no row has come back.

prompt: `SELECT count(*) FROM sharded_orders WHERE seller_id = 42` took 262 ms and the same count for customer 42 took 39 ms. What does the plan show for the seller?
hint: Seller is not the key.

choices.text: One Foreign Scan, on the shard holding seller 42
choices.why: Seller 42's orders are on both shards, because the split is by customer.

choices.text: No WHERE in the remote SQL: every row comes back
choices.why: The WHERE does travel; each shard filters, but reads its whole table to do it.

choices.text: A sequential scan of the coordinator's own orders
choices.why: The coordinator holds no order rows in sharded_orders.

choices.text: An Append over both shards, each sent the same WHERE
choices.why: Right: the query fans out, and each shard scans without an index on seller_id.

prompt: Why did `GROUP BY status` over the shards take 2961 ms against 565 ms locally, even with `enable_partitionwise_aggregate`?
hint: Each shard holds part of every status.

choices.text: Because status is a text column, and the coordinator has no way to count text on a remote server
choices.why: Grouping by customer_id was pushed down; the type is not the issue.

choices.text: Two million values crossed the wire, since PostgreSQL 16 sends no partial counts down
choices.why: Right: only a grouping by the key, where each shard's count is final, ran on the shards.

choices.text: Because the coordinator had not been analysed, so it guessed the shards were empty and planned badly
choices.why: It was analysed after the load; the plan still pulled the rows.

choices.text: Because shard1 holds more orders than shard2
choices.why: They hold 995080 and 1004920, close to even, and shard2 holds slightly more.

prompt: How many orders hold the id 1 after the `INSERT` of order 1 for customer 3 through the coordinator?
hint: The INSERT was routed by customer, not by id.

prompt: Both COMMITs in the section print the same duplicate-key error. What makes the first one worse than the second?
hint: Look at what was left on shard1 afterwards.

choices.text: The first left order 2000001 committed on shard1 although the coordinator reported failure
choices.why: Right: shard1 committed before shard2 refused, so half the transaction survived.

choices.text: The first rolled back both shards, while the second left the rows it wrote committed on shard2
choices.why: It is the reverse: the second left nothing, the first left a row.

choices.text: The first was slower
choices.why: Timing is not the problem; a committed half is.

choices.text: The first used two-phase commit and the second did not
choices.why: postgres_fdw in PostgreSQL 16 uses two-phase commit for neither.

prompt: Which of these did a single `orders` table give you that the two shards in the section did not? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three things stopped working.

choices.text: A unique index on `id`
choices.why: Right: PostgreSQL refuses it on a table with foreign partitions.

choices.text: A transaction that commits everywhere or nowhere
choices.why: Right: one shard committed and the other refused.

choices.text: A cheap aggregate grouped by any column
choices.why: Right: grouping by status pulled two million values over the wire.

choices.text: Routing an INSERT to the right place
choices.why: Routing worked: each order went to the shard its customer hashes to.

choices.text: A query for one customer that reads one shard
choices.why: That worked: customer 42 was pruned to one Foreign Scan.

prompt: Going from 2 hash shards to 4, how much of `orders` has to move?
hint: The capture counted 999306.

choices.text: About a quarter
choices.why: 999306 of 2000000 is half, not a quarter.

choices.text: None, because the old shards keep their rows
choices.why: Each old shard hands half its rows to a new one.

choices.text: About half
choices.why: Right: 999306 of 2000000, while the application keeps writing.

choices.text: All of it, because every hash changes
choices.why: The hash of a key does not change; only which remainder is taken.

prompt: After `ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN coupon text` ran on both shards, the coordinator still said `column "coupon" does not exist`. Why?
hint: Who describes the shards to the coordinator?

choices.text: The ALTER on the shards had not committed yet when the coordinator ran its query
choices.why: Each psql -c commits on its own; the shards had the column.

choices.text: A foreign table cannot have columns added
choices.why: ALTER TABLE on the coordinator added it, and the query worked.

choices.text: The shards cached the old definition for a minute
choices.why: The shards were right; the coordinator was out of date.

choices.text: Its foreign tables describe the shards as they were, until it is altered too
choices.why: Right: a schema change is one statement per shard plus one on the coordinator.

prompt: Why do teams that shard often create 64 logical shards on 2 machines?
hint: Think about the day a third machine arrives.

choices.text: A new server then receives whole pieces instead of rehashed rows
choices.why: Right: a logical shard moves intact, and no row needs a new hash.

choices.text: PostgreSQL needs one partition per processor
choices.why: There is no such rule.

choices.text: Smaller shards remove the hot shard
choices.why: A single hot key stays on one shard however small the shards are.

choices.text: It makes cross-shard transactions atomic
choices.why: Atomicity needs two-phase commit, not more shards.

prompt: Two shards are backed up every night at 02:00, one after the other, and each backup takes an hour. A restore of both is attempted. What is the lesson's concern?
hint: Two pictures, two moments.

choices.text: The second backup will be twice as large
choices.why: Size is not the problem; the moment each one shows is.

choices.text: Restoring both will take at least two hours, which is longer than the night's maintenance window
choices.why: Duration matters, but the lesson's point is consistency between shards.

choices.text: The shards come back at different moments, with cross-shard transactions cut in half
choices.why: Right: a consistent restore needs every shard recovered to the same instant from archived WAL.

choices.text: Backups of a sharded database are impossible
choices.why: They are possible; they need coordination across shards.

prompt: Match each id scheme for a sharded table with its cost.
hint: The table in section 05.

pairs.right: larger indexes, inserts all over the index
the number of shards baked into the ids
a single point every write depends on

right_distractors: ids that two shards may hand out twice

prompt: A team runs Citus and picked `seller_id` as the distribution column for orders. A quarter of orders are one seller's. What does Citus change about the problem?
hint: The lesson lists what Citus carries and what it does not.

choices.text: It splits the big seller's orders across several workers automatically
choices.why: A distribution column sends one value to one shard; Citus does not split a value.

choices.text: It switches the distribution column to customer_id when it detects skew
choices.why: Citus never chooses the key; the team does.

choices.text: It makes transactions atomic across shards, and the hot shard remains
choices.why: Right: two-phase commit is on its list; choosing the key is not.

choices.text: It removes the need for a shard key
choices.why: Every distributed table has a distribution column.
